items.title: “Should I Give Up Now?” Investigating LLM Pitfalls in Software Engineering
items.abstract: Software engineers are increasingly incorporating AI assistants into their workflows to enhance productivity and alleviate cognitive load. However, experiences with Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT vary widely. While some engineers find them useful, others deem them counterproductive due to inaccuracies in their responses. Researchers have also observed that ChatGPT often provides incorrect information. Given these limitations, it is crucial to determine how to effectively integrate LLMs into Software Engineering (SE) workflow. Analyzing data from 26 participants in a complex web development task, we identified nine failure types categorized into incorrect or incomplete responses, cognitive overload, and context loss. Users attempted to mitigate these issues through scaffolding, prompt clarification, and debugging. However, 17 participants ultimately chose to abandon ChatGPT due to persistent failures. Our quantitative analysis revealed that unhelpful responses increased the likelihood of abandonment by a factor of 11, while each additional prompt reduced abandonment probability by 17%. This study advances the understanding of human-AI interaction in SE tasks and outlines directions for future research and tooling support.

items.title: $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling
items.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

items.title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
items.abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

items.title: 5 Critical Threat Scenarios for Rogue AI Attacks on Europe's Critical Digital Infrastructure and Possible Mitigation
items.abstract: Alternative Titles: AI Security: 5 Critical Threat Scenarios Where an AI Agent’s Permission Is Not Authorization Top 5 Rogue AI Threat Scenarios: Binding Consequential AI Actions to Independent Authorization in Critical Infrastructure AI Safety for NIS2 and the EU AI Act: 5 Threat Models and an Enforcement Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents Abstract Autonomous AI agents, optimizers, and AI-assisted security tools now hold standing permissions to alter production infrastructure at machine speed. In the European Union, this is no longer merely a technical vulnerability—it is a strict regulatory compliance mandate. Operators of essential and important entities under the NIS2 Directive, financial entities under DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act), critical entities under the CER Directive, and providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act must definitively prove that automated actions cannot cause uncontrolled, cascading disruptions. While conventional cybersecurity controls—such as AI guardrails, Role-Based Access Control (IAM/RBAC), LLM-as-a-judge reviewer models, human approval workflows, canary releases, and anomaly detection tools—reduce risk, none of them structurally prevent a wrong, manipulated, or malicious AI decision from becoming an effective infrastructure change. This technical disclosure analyzes the persistent "guardrail trap" and introduces a non-bypassable architectural solution. This disclosure defines a comprehensive threat model featuring 5 critical rogue-AI scenarios: The Runaway Optimizer: A locally optimal AI decision triggers systemic infrastructure instability. Unmediated Agentic Execution: A privileged AI assistant converts an ambiguous instruction into a destructive operation. Correlated Security Monoculture: Shared AI security logic causes synchronized, false-positive network shutdowns. Adversarially Induced Infrastructure Shutdown: External attackers manipulate automated defenses into disabling essential services (e.g., via prompt injection or data poisoning). The Self-Authorizing Agent: A rogue agent edits its own guardrails, forges its approval, and erases its audit logs. To address these vulnerabilities, the disclosure details 51 threat variations, a 36-entry threat register, and 12 required security properties for autonomous systems. It provides a qualitative comparison demonstrating which common control classes meet these properties. Crucially, it establishes a formal technical distinction between permission (a standing, class-level entitlement) and authorization (a one-time, act-specific, state-bound capability consumed on use), as well as separating a "pending" workflow status from a cryptographically enforced "non-effective state." The Protected Execution-Finality Architecture: The proposed safeguard ensures that every consequential AI action remains in a non-effective state until an Independent Validator reconstructs the actual pending operation and issues a single-use capability bound to that exact act. A Policy Enforcement Point (Finality Sink) at the real point of effect verifies the capability, rejecting stale, substituted, replayed, or widened operations. For high-criticality environments, the architecture introduces receipt-gated staged effectuation (Interim Effectuation Validation), ensuring that even a mistakenly authorized change exposes only the current stage, gated by destination-generated cryptographic evidence. The disclosure provides consequence-tiered latency rules, fail-closed behaviors during validator outages, 20 defensive simulation blueprints with acceptance criteria, and explicit residual limits. All scenarios are hypothetical threat models, not reports of incidents, and no experimental results are claimed. European Regulatory Mapping: This architecture's relevance is mapped directly to European compliance frameworks: EU AI Act: Risk management systems (Article 9), human oversight (Article 14), robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), and automatic logging (Article 12). NIS2 & DORA: ICT risk management, supply chain security, and incident containment. items.title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
items.abstract: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: From Foundations to Frontiers
items.abstract: Large Language Models demonstrate strong generative capabilities but remain constrained by static training data, susceptibility to hallucination, and an inability to access current or domain-specific information at inference time. RetrievalAugmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling language models with external retrieval mechanisms that dynamically supply relevant knowledge during generation. In the years since its introduction, RAG has expanded from a single architecture into a broad ecosystem of retrieval modalities, architectural variants, and deployment patterns that is increasingly difficult to navigate. This survey provides a unified treatment of that landscape, organized around five retrieval paradigms: sparse lexical retrieval, structured data retrieval, dense semantic retrieval, graph-enhanced retrieval, and agentic retrieval. For each paradigm, we trace the evolution from foundational concepts to current practice, examining the core techniques, architectural patterns, and design trade-offs that practitioners face. Cutting across these paradigms, we examine two disciplines that shape every RAG system: context management, which governs how retrieved information is selected, compressed, and presented to the generator, and evaluation, which measures retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and end-to-end system performance. To make techniques comparable across paradigms, we ground each in a shared vocabulary for the stages of a RAG pipeline and consolidate representative works along five recurring dimensions: retrieval stage, generation stage, system properties, trust and governance, and adaptability. Our analysis reveals that significant challenges persist. Hallucination is reduced but not eliminated, and retrieval augmentation can mask it from standard detectors. Retrieval quality remains highly sensitive to domain and query complexity. Effective use of long contexts lags behind the rapid growth of context window sizes. Automated evaluation metrics often diverge from real-world user satisfaction. We discuss these open problems alongside promising research directions, including multi-modal and federated architectures, cost-efficient graph systems, and standardized governance frameworks. Together, this survey offers a structured road map for researchers and practitioners navigating this rapidly evolving field.

items.title: A decade‐scale audit of microbiome AI‐readiness
items.abstract: A systematic, PRISMA-guided review led by our consortium screened 23,781 human microbiome papers and procured 2896 studies published from 2012 to 2025 that were then scored by reviewers into four Biological Host-Associated AI-Ready Metadata (BHAM) tiers. Only 5.9% of studies deposited sequence data with per-sample host disease status, age, and sex, and 63.1% shared no reusable sequence data, so that 85.5% of roughly 720,000 samples cannot be reused for cross-cohort or artificial intelligence (AI) analyses without contacting the authors. Sequence deposition improved modestly over time, whereas per-sample annotation did not. Journals, repositories, and researchers should require structured, machine-readable metadata at submission, supported by AI-assisted curation.

items.title: A Fairness-Aware Explainable Artificial Intelligence Clinical Decision Support Framework Using Electronic Health Records
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) are increasingly being adopted in Electronic Health Record (EHR) based healthcare settings to enhance disease prediction, clinical diagnosis and operational efficiency. Current healthcare AI systems, however, are facing serious challenges such as demographic bias, transparency, unreliable predictions, poor explainability and low clinician trust. We propose a fairness-aware explainable AI framework for trustworthy and transparent EHR-based CDSS. The proposed framework integrates machine learning prediction models with SHAP-based explainability, fairness evaluation metrics, subgroup bias attribution, reliability testing, and clinician-centered evaluation into one trustworthy healthcare AI architecture. Experiments are done using standard EHR datasets like UCI Heart Disease Dataset and MIMIC-IV. We compared different models like Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost using metrics such as accuracy, ROC-AUC, Equalized Odds, Demographic Parity, robustness score and explainability consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the reliability of clinical prediction, reduces subgroup bias, enhances interpretability, and increases clinician trust compared to conventional black-box healthcare AI systems. This work advances towards trustworthy, transparent, and fairness-aware healthcare AI systems fit for real-world clinical deployment.

items.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

items.title: A fragmented field in transition: knowledge structures and emerging agendas in lifelong learning for sustainable development
items.abstract: Lifelong learning is increasingly recognised as essential to sustainable development, yet its knowledge structure and emerging research directions remain insufficiently understood. This study analysed 806 articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection between 2001 and 30 July 2026 using bibliometric, collaboration-network, keyword co-occurrence, temporal-comparison, and sensitivity analyses. The findings revealed sustained publication growth, fragmented author collaboration, and uneven institutional connectivity. Two major thematic concentrations emerged: transformative and sustainability education in higher education and teacher development; and adult, non-formal, informal, community, and continuing learning associated with the Sustainable Development Goals. Emerging research directions included inclusive education, experiential learning, sustainability competencies, gender equality, gamification, and artificial intelligence, although these remained relatively low-frequency topics. Sensitivity analysis indicated that keyword-network coherence was partly influenced by the retrieval strategy. Overall, the literature demonstrated growing interest in participatory, inclusive, competency-oriented, and digitally supported learning while remaining structurally dispersed. This study clarifies the intellectual landscape of lifelong learning for sustainable development, identifies emerging research priorities, and emphasises the importance of retrieval design when interpreting bibliometric findings.

items.title: A graph attention network-driven multi-omics framework for predicting infection severity and therapeutic outcomes in diabetes
items.abstract: Introduction Diabetes mellitus predisposes patients to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections owing to impaired immune responses and metabolic dysfunction, frequently leading to severe complications, prolonged hospitalization, and suboptimal therapeutic outcomes. Accurate risk stratification remains challenging due to the heterogeneous and high-dimensional nature of multi-omics data, which hinders effective integration across molecular layers. Methods To address this gap, we propose a graph attention network (GAT)-based multi-omics integration framework that jointly models genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and clinical variables for predicting infection severity and treatment outcomes in diabetic patients. A retrospective multicenter cohort of 2,800 diabetic patients was assembled, encompassing 18,500 genomic variants, 19,800 transcriptomic features, 4,250 proteomic features, 610 metabolites, 320 microbial taxa, and 28 clinical variables. Infection severity was categorized into four clinically defined levels: mild (n = 720), moderate (n = 940), severe (n = 760), and critical (n = 380). After preprocessing, 43,508 molecular features were reduced to 1,024 optimized biomarkers through a sequential pipeline of differential expression analysis, mutual information filtering, LASSO regression, and recursive feature elimination. A heterogeneous patient similarity graph comprising 2,800 nodes and approximately 96,400 weighted edges was constructed using cosine similarity. A three-layer graph attention network with eight attention heads per layer generated 256-dimensional node embeddings, which were subsequently utilized in a multi-task learning framework to jointly predict infection severity and therapeutic outcome. The proposed framework was evaluated via five-fold cross-validation and benchmarked against conventional machine learning models (SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP) and graph-based deep learning models (GCN, GraphSAGE). Results The GAT-based model achieved an accuracy of 98.34%, precision of 97.86%, recall of 97.63%, specificity of 98.11%, F1-score of 97.74%, Matthews correlation coefficient of 96.95%, AUC of 99.18%, and AUPRC of 98.82%, significantly outperforming all baseline models. Discussion These results demonstrate that the proposed GNN-driven multi-omics framework effectively integrates heterogeneous molecular and clinical information, offering a promising artificial intelligence-assisted precision medicine tool for personalized risk stratification, therapeutic decision-making, and improved clinical management of infections in diabetic patients.

items.title: A Hybrid Retrieval and Reranking Framework for Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves the reliability of large language model outputs by grounding generated responses in external evidence. However, the quality of RAG-generated answers depends strongly on the relevance of retrieved evidence, the effectiveness of evidence ranking, and the ability to verify whether generated claims are supported by source documents. This study presents a hybrid retrieval and reranking framework for citation-aware RAG in biomedical and healthcare-related document question answering. The proposed framework uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases for document ingestion, parsing, chunking, embedding generation, and evidence retrieval. Source PDF documents are stored in Amazon S3, embedded using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, and indexed using Amazon OpenSearch Serverless. A hybrid retrieval strategy is applied to retrieve candidate evidence chunks, followed by reranking to prioritize the most relevant passages before answer generation. The answer-generation stage uses the highest-ranked evidence chunks to produce controlled, evidence-grounded responses, while a separate judge model evaluates each generated factual claim against the retrieved evidence. The framework was evaluated using 150 biomedical natural language processing and healthcare transformer queries. This evaluation was designed as a pilot-scale proof-of-concept study to examine the feasibility of the proposed hybrid retrieval, reranking, answer-generation, and grounding-evaluation workflow. Across the evaluation set, the system retrieved and reranked 3,000 evidence chunks and generated responses from the top-ranked evidence. Claim-level grounding evaluation identified 1,200 factual claims, of which 1,184 were judged to be supported by the retrieved evidence and 16 were classified as unsupported, resulting in an overall grounding accuracy of 98.7%. The results indicate that hybrid retrieval, reranking, conservative prompting, and claim-level grounding evaluation can support reliable evidence-grounded RAG responses when sufficient source evidence is available. The study also highlights the distinction between internal grounding accuracy and strict citation accuracy, motivating future work on explicit sentence-level citation generation and expanded human expert validation.

items.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
items.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.

items.title: A multilayer ontology of psychological stress ranging from lived experiences to neurobiological cascades
items.abstract: Chronic stress is a phenomenon measured in pieces: an appraised predicament, a behavioral pattern, an autonomic shift, an HPA-axis cascade, an inflammatory-metabolic state, a molecular signature. Each is well characterized, but they are rarely reconciled in one computable model. We present the Corticoidogenic Stress Frames (CSF), a modular ontology network in which eight conceptual frames are each anchored to a primary corticoidogenic literature. CSF formalizes eight stress-related strata with their pathways and the cascade steps occurring at each layer. Appropriate competency questions validate the result on knowledge graphs extracted from stress-related datasets. CSF-shaped knowledge graphs are extracted automatically either from physiological data or linguistic reports. The extraction is performed by POLANYI++, a neurosymbolic AI pipeline in which a LLM recognizes patterns, while the ontology supplies the inductive bias, the vocabulary and the validation. Sensor features and first-person narrative bind to shared cascade steps, so quantified physiology and appraisal data are represented in a graph, while keeping their provenance. We present six studies. Study 0 confirms on a signal-free dataset that the pipeline returns a null rather than fabricating structure. Study 1 shows CSF constructs are sensitive to known conditions across three benchmarks. Study 2 finds a within-subject coupling between daily activity and momentary stress, positive within individuals, yet dissociable from the protective trait-level exercise buffer of Study 1. Study 3 evaluates extraction from forty-one unannotated diary posts by a reverse method, extracting the conceptual frames convergent with model-free affect signals. Study 4 shows that the co-activation distribution over multilayer frames is stable. In Study 5, five models from three families judge extraction items under blinding, aggregated by a Dawid–Skene latent-class model. By design each specialist rules only within its own stratum and abstains elsewhere, which keeps the judgments free of cross-expertise contamination. As an external human referent, a neuropsychologist rated a sample, endorsing the extracted frames in 11 of 13 cases. The framework offers a route to layer integration in stress physiology, with evidential status of each layer represented explicitly.

items.title: A Place in Between
items.abstract: A Place in Between is a 4-minute-7-second black-and-white short film about memory, absence, hope, and the emotional space between holding on and letting go. The project was realized through a director-led sequential workflow that combined iterative story and storyboard development, still-image generation, image-to-video synthesis, and conventional post-production. ChatGPT supported iterative story, storyboard, and prompt development; GPT Image 2, Nano Banana Pro, and Nano Banana 2 were used to create still frames; and Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0 were used exclusively in image-to-video mode. Sprite and reference sheets anchored recurring character identities. Each shot passed through multiple generations, human selection, and retouching before motion synthesis. Adobe Premiere Pro and After Effects were used for editorial construction, stabilization, masking, compositing, tonal finishing, sound design, and mastering. The resulting workflow shows how generative systems can operate inside a conventional directorial process while narrative intention, continuity, performance, rhythm, and final assembly remain under human control.

items.title: A Reflection-Grounded Framework for AI Workflows and Assessment in Design Education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce polished personas, visual concepts, interface layouts, and design outputs, making final artefacts an increasingly unreliable indicator of students’ design understanding and contribution. This paper examines how assessment in design education can move beyond visual outcomes to evaluate the capabilities students exercise when working with generative AI. The study analyses 80 beginning-of-semester concept submissions and 79 end-of-semester reflections from an undergraduate design course, including 77 matched student pairs. Crucially, this setup allowed us to trace how workflows evolved as students transitioned from a mandated-AI conceptual phase to a free-choice prototyping phase. Through inductive coding and cross-stage qualitative comparison, findings show that students valued AI as a cognitive partner for early divergent exploration. However, many deliberately abandoned it during high-fidelity execution due to limited directability, generic outputs, cultural misrepresentation, and inefficiency. Based on these trajectories, we propose an assessment framework mapped to the Double Diamond design process. This framework derives seven assessable AI-era capabilities, enabling educators to evaluate design judgment, verification, and ethical responsibility rather than generated outputs alone.

items.title: A Review of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Implications for Employment and Economic Inequality
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming work environments through automated task execution, content generation, data analysis, and human–AI collaboration. This review examines its technological foundations, workplace adoption, implications for employment, and potential effects on economic inequality. It outlines major generative architectures, including generative adversarial networks, transformers, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, autoencoders, and autoregressive models, as well as applications in image, audio, video, and three-dimensional content generation. The review then considers how technological capabilities translate into employment outcomes through firm adoption, deployment depth, task reorganization, complementary investment, and labor reallocation. It also discusses the changing skills required in AI-enabled workplaces, emphasizing critical thinking, creativity, emotional intelligence, digital literacy, AI ethics, and human–machine collaboration. Furthermore, the paper explores how unequal access to AI technologies, occupational disruption, and concentrated economic benefits may widen disparities within and between countries. Ethical, security, bias, privacy, and interpretability challenges are also considered. Overall, the review highlights the need for workforce development, responsible AI governance, inclusive policies, and equitable access to ensure that GenAI supports productive, broadly shared socioeconomic progress across diverse sectors and communities amid changing economic conditions.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Systems Model of Remote Maritime Operations: Total Interpretive Structural Modelling of Human Capability, Situation Awareness and Navigation Safety
items.abstract: The shift to Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship (MASS) operations redistributes safety-critical functions among Remote Operation Centre (ROC) navigators, automation and digital systems. Yet, relationships among Operator Capability, cognition, work-system conditions and Navigation Safety remain insufficiently integrated. This study develops a literature-grounded socio-technical model using a 48-study systematic literature review, thematic synthesis, Total Interpretive Structural Modelling (TISM), MICMAC analysis, structural sensitivity analysis and preliminary expert review. Retrospective eligibility reassessment and author-confirmed source verification finalised the 48-study evidence base; historical screening and coding provenance was partially reconstructed. Eight elements were retained: Operator Capability, Situation Awareness (SA), Decision-Making Quality, Navigation Safety, Human–Machine Interface and Information/Data Conditions, Workload, Trust and Transparency, and Level of Automation. The six-level hierarchy places automation upstream of interface/information conditions; Operator Capability, workload and trust/transparency; SA; decision making; and Navigation Safety. SA is a cognitive state supporting decision making, with selected human and system conditions also modelled as direct influences. Downstream ordering persisted across contextual alternatives but changed when decision-making-to-SA feedback merged SA and decision making. The model represents structural reachability, not empirically established causality, mediation or predictive validity. Preliminary expert review informed refinement, not empirical validation. The model supports Goal-Directed Task Analysis, competency mapping and simulator-based ROC assessment.

items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
items.abstract: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: A Survey on Image Restoration in the Foundation Model Era
items.abstract: Foundation models provide transferable representations, generative priors, and multimodal understanding, offering new ways to address diverse image degradations and restoration requirements. This survey reviews three complementary directions: leveraging existing foundation models for image restoration, developing restoration-oriented foundation models, and coordinating restoration models and tools through agents. We examine how pretrained representations, generative priors, and additional supervision support image restoration. For restoration-oriented foundation models, we compare pretraining, unified modeling, and adaptation strategies across tasks and domains. For agentic image restoration, we examine how agents coordinate restoration models and tools within a unified framework for diverse tasks through task planning, tool selection, feedback-driven refinement, and experience retrieval. We summarize reported benchmark results and model budgets to examine the strengths and limitations of existing methods, taking into account differences in training coverage, adaptation, and evaluation settings. Finally, we discuss challenges and future directions in generalization and adaptation to real-world degradations, faithful and user-controllable restoration, reliable assessment for agents, and efficient and reproducible deployment. A curated list of works reviewed in this survey is available at https://github.com/mrluin/Awesome-IR-in-FM-era.

items.title: A Survey on Machine Learning Techniques for Building Advanced Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) represents an emerging paradigm in artificial intelligence that enables systems to operate autonomously, adapt to dynamic environments, and pursue complex goals with minimal human intervention. Unlike traditional AI systems that rely on predefined rules and supervised execution, Agentic AI integrates perception, reasoning, learning, and action to make intelligent decisions in real time. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Agentic AI systems, focusing on their architectural foundations, learning paradigms, and emerging application domains. The study examines key architectural frameworks, highlighting their capabilities and limitations. The paper also reviews recent advancements and applications of Agentic AI in manufacturing, cybersecurity, healthcare, enterprise automation, and distributed systems. A comparative analysis of existing literature identifies critical research gaps related to scalability, explainability, security, governance, and human–AI collaboration. This survey provides a structured overview of the current state of Agentic AI and serves as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand its architectures, capabilities, and application potential

items.title: A$^3$Bench: Compositional Reasoning over Aggressive Interactions in Videos
items.abstract: Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on general video understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to reason about participant roles in aggressive interactions remains largely unexplored. Existing violence and crime datasets primarily evaluate whether aggression occurs, without testing whether models can identify who performed the action, who received it, and how participants are related within the scene. To address this gap, we introduce A$^3$Bench, a benchmark to study aggressive action and association in videos. The benchmark evaluates whether models can jointly recognize aggressive actions, distinguish aggressors from victims and bystanders, and correctly bind actions to participants under challenging distractor settings. We benchmark 17 multimodal models and find that they struggle substantially on fine-grained aggressive-scene understanding. Performance degrades consistently as reasoning complexity increases, with models frequently confusing aggressors with victims or bystanders, revealing a systematic failure in role-action association rather than coarse aggression recognition alone. We further observe that increasing model scale or generic reasoning models experience limited improvement. Finally, we explore a simple role-graph prompting strategy that encourages structured reasoning over participant interactions, leading to improvements in compositional reasoning. Our findings highlight that reliable aggressive-scene understanding remains a major challenge for current MLLMs and motivate future research on role-aware video reasoning beyond coarse violence detection. Code and dataset: https://github.com/austincbaker/A3Bench.

items.title: Adaptability and Adaptivity in Manual Assembly Systems: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The expanding array of production variants and the shifting demographic and organizational landscapes demand flexible and adaptable assembly systems. In this context, adaptive systems that can dynamically adapt to changing requirements, user groups, and contextual conditions offer considerable potential. This study aims to analyze the current state of research on adaptive and adaptable manual assembly systems by conducting a systematic literature review (SLR). The objective of this analysis is twofold: first, to identify key influencing factors, and second, to determine existing research gaps. The findings of the present study indicate that previous research has predominantly centered on technological and ergonomic aspects, particularly cyber-physical systems, assistive technologies, and anthropometric workplace adaptation. Conversely, psychosocial influencing factors, such as individual stress, strain, and qualification diversity, have received minimal attention. The failure to consider these human-related variables represents a significant research gap, particularly with regard to the sustainable design of adaptive systems. A discrepancy emerges between the theoretical conceptualization of the concepts and their practical implementation. The study underscores the imperative for interdisciplinary research, integrating technical, psychological, and organizational perspectives, to achieve the full potential of adaptive systems. In summary, the text presents a series of specific recommendations for the advancement of adaptive manual assembly systems in both research and practice.

items.title: Advances in Understanding and Managing Cadmium Contamination in Rice: Mechanisms and Management Strategies
items.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a highly toxic, non-essential heavy metal and a widespread soil contaminant in rice-growing regions worldwide, posing significant threats to food safety, environmental quality, and human health. Rice (Oryza sativa L.), a staple food for more than half of the world’s population, readily absorbs Cd from contaminated soils and can accumulate substantial amounts in its grains, making it a major contributor to dietary Cd exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in rice Cd contamination research, with a particular focus on Cd uptake and transport mechanisms, phytotoxic effects, contamination sources, and mitigation strategies. Current progress in agronomic management, in situ immobilization, bioremediation, low-Cd rice breeding, and molecular approaches is critically examined, highlighting advances in genome editing, membrane transporter biology, and omics-based functional genomics. Emerging technologies, including CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing, ion homeostasis engineering, pan-genome analysis, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted precision management, are opening new avenues for developing low-Cd rice cultivars and improving contamination control. By integrating genetic improvement with climate-resilient cultivation practices, this review outlines a preventive, integrated, and sustainable framework for Cd risk mitigation in rice production systems. It also identifies key research gaps and future priorities to support the development of safer rice varieties, optimize Cd management strategies, and enhance the sustainability of rice production under changing environmental conditions.

items.title: Advancing a FAIR and explainable AI-based predictive model for cardiovascular diseases in hospital settings
items.abstract: The healthcare field is witnessing an increasing volume of data available for analysis and is undergoing pragmatic transformations due to the advent of artificial intelligence. In recent years, machine learning and its sub-field, deep learning have emerged as effective tools to help physicians with diagnosis, predictions and improved treatment plans. The paper describes a cohort of patients which were monitored during their regular visits in the cardiology department of the County Emergency Clinical Hospital of Timis in Romania on their physiological parameters and test results. After employing a wide range of conventional machine learning and advanced deep learning techniques, the experimental results revealed that the feedforward neural network performed best in predicting cardiovascular outcomes. The paper also analyzes the aspects of FAIR AI, which translates to the usage of artificial intelligence in a ethical and unbiased way in order to improve the early and precise diagnosis for cardiac patients. The work presented in this paper represents an overview of the current situation in CVDs management and treatment options, as well as offering a viable and interoperable AI-based solution that can be integrated in cardiology hospital departments in order to improve the diagnosis and experience of cardiac patients.

items.title: Agentic AI Security for Europe: After Fugaku and Google's Autonomous Hacking Agent, Why Valid Credentials Must Not Be Enough to Change a Supercomputer, Cloud or Critical System
items.abstract: Europe is building and relying on supercomputers, cloud platforms and AI agents that act at machine speed, and two public reports from November 2026 show how fast apparently valid access can become real damage. RIKEN reported that an external party entered Japan’s Fugaku supercomputer network through a publicly reachable status dashboard, tampered with internal servers and may have obtained account credentials, including SSH keys. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported autonomous multi-agent hacking frameworks, including an exposed framework called exploit_agent that drafts and runs exploits without a human approving each step, plus cloud-credential abuse such as LLMJacking. Google’s telemetry also suggested attention to certain French websites. These are separate events, and no public evidence links them or shows AI use at Fugaku. This paper asks what a defender can still do after a firewall, login or AI guardrail has been passed. It explains where conventional controls (zero trust, IAM, endpoint detection, AI guardrails, human approval) reach their limits, without dismissing them. It then describes a defender-controlled pre-commit enforcement point (a reference monitor, or commit gate) that holds a proposed operation in a non-effective state until its actual target, scope, destination and current authority are independently checked. That reduces what a stolen key, a compromised dashboard or a manipulated AI agent can actually change, release or provision. For the European context, the paper maps the approach to: EuroHPC-style supercomputing and research data; the NIS2 Directive (risk-management measures and incident handling); the EU AI Act (cybersecurity and robustness of high-risk AI systems, and human oversight); DORA (ICT risk in financial entities); the Cyber Resilience Act; and GDPR security of processing and personal-data-breach exposure, which is directly relevant because the Fugaku notice concerned possible leakage of users’ personal information. It also includes 17 diagrams, a counterfactual Fugaku analysis, AI-agent and cloud-abuse scenarios, ten falsifiable experiments, a comparison with conventional systems and 52 FAQs. It states its limits plainly. It does not claim the approach was deployed at Fugaku, would have prevented the breach, has been benchmarked, or guarantees regulatory compliance. Based on the Mothership application PCT/IB2026/055615, filed 4 June 2026 and publicly disclosed 16 July 2026. The underlying invention is human-originated. AI-assisted tools were used to summarize the filing and draft the threat scenarios, comparisons and regulatory and industry-relevance material, so the paper may contain errors, and readers must cross-check it against the original public sources. The regulatory mapping is AI-generated and is not legal advice. The company alignment (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft) is AI-generated, is not an endorsement, validation or infringement statement, and must be cross-checked against the original PCT filing before any conclusion is drawn. items.title: Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey of Foundations, Architectural Paradigms, Core Capabilities, and a Unified Reference Architecture
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) integrates goal-directed decision-making, state continuity, planning, tool-mediated action, and feedback-driven adaptation into interactive computational systems. Although existing surveys examine agent capabilities, architectures, and applications, cross-paradigm comparisons often conflate functional capabilities with implementation mechanisms and organizational structures. This comprehensive narrative survey synthesizes foundational and contemporary research on symbolic/classical, neural/generative, neuro-symbolic, and multi-agent approaches to clarify conceptual boundaries and examine how agentic capabilities are architecturally realized. It organizes recurring functions into nine groups: goal and context management, perception and state representation, reasoning and decision-making, planning and replanning, memory and knowledge, action and tool use, evaluation and reflection, learning and adaptation, and coordination and orchestration. The principal contribution is an architecture-capability mapping separating functional responsibilities from computational mechanisms and coordination structures. A complementary conceptual reference architecture integrates goal management, environmental interaction, planning, memory, execution, evaluation, and cross-cutting assurance concerns. Representative cases demonstrate how different systems can realize similar functions using different mechanisms. The proposed taxonomy, formal abstraction, and reference architecture are analytical synthesis artifacts rather than experimentally validated models. They support transparent architectural comparison and identify testable research questions.

items.title: Agentic workflows in large language models: a comprehensive review of architectures, planning strategies, and real-world applications
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agentic workflows: systems in which an LLM plans tasks, retains memory, uses external tools, and coordinates with other agents to complete multi-step objectives. Existing surveys typically evaluate these components in isolation or rely on flat, mutually exclusive categorizations that conflate coordination patterns with functional roles and tooling. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review synthesizes 126 Scopus-indexed, peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2023 and June 2026, with screening conducted by a single reviewer. Because 122 of these articles appeared in 2025 and 2026, the corpus provides a timely, peer-evaluated evidence base for this rapidly accelerating field. Across seven research questions, we introduce a multi-layered taxonomy whose explicit novelty lies in strictly decoupling three primary coordination topologies (single-agent, collaborative multi-agent, and hierarchical supervisory) from orthogonal functional dimensions (role specialization), cross-cutting capability layers (tool augmentation and hybrid memory), and governance mechanisms (human-in-the-loop). Unlike prior rigid taxonomies that force systems into a single category, this structural separation systematically models modern hybrid implementations by combining distinct operational layers without artificial pigeonholing. Among the 57 empirical studies, collaborative multi-agent organization was the most frequently observed identifiable primary topology (27 studies, representing 47.4% of the empirical subset [ n = 27/57] and 21.4% of the total 126-study corpus). Across software engineering, healthcare, cybersecurity, and robotics, most reported implementations remain controlled research prototypes. Practical autonomy continues to be constrained by pipeline-level vulnerabilities: compounding error propagation, indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, and the lack of standardized trajectory-level benchmarks. To advance agentic workflows toward dependable deployment, future research must prioritize standardized long-horizon evaluation, capability-based security architectures, and controlled self-evolution.

items.title: Agricultural labour and drug use: insights from list experiments in Nigeria
items.abstract: Background The world is facing a severe drug crisis, posing serious public health and societal risks. Yet, little is known about drug use among farmers and farmworkers, despite their essential role in global food production. This knowledge gap is particularly concerning because poor mental health and precarious working conditions are common in agriculture and may be associated with drug use as a coping mechanism, a relationship observed in other settings. However, evidence from agriculture remains extremely limited, largely due to data gaps. One challenge in collecting such data is social desirability bias, stemming from the topic’s sensitivity. We address this gap by using sensitive question techniques and provide novel evidence on drug use among farmers and farmworkers and its association with working conditions and work-related health. Methods We conducted item-count and item-sum double list experiments with 1,554 farmers and hired farmworkers between July and August 2023 to measure the prevalence and frequency of non-medical drug use in Nigeria’s labour-intensive tomato sector. Substances included cannabis, opioid painkillers such as tramadol and codeine, cough syrups, and similar drugs. List experiments avoid direct questioning and can estimate sensitive behaviours while hiding respondents’ answers from the interviewer. Using these estimates, we ran multivariate regressions on residualised outcome variables to identify work-related risk factors associated with drug use, focusing on burnout, work-related pain and health problems, pesticide exposure, unusual working hours, and belief in work performance effects. Results The item-count experiment suggests that about 8% of farmers, 20% of seasonal workers, and 6% of casual workers used drugs in the previous 12 months. The item-sum experiment estimates that drug-using farmers and seasonal workers consumed drugs on average about 8 days in the previous month, compared with about 7 days among drug-using casual workers. Multivariate regression analyses show that work-related pain and belief in performance-enhancing effects are the most important risk factors for frequent drug use. Our results also demonstrate that burnout levels are significantly higher among farmworkers than among farmers, but we do not find a significant association between work-related burnout and drug use. Conclusions Farmers and farmworkers suffer from important occupational health deficits. Drug use and mental health in rural areas in particular remain underappreciated on policy and research agendas. Implications for agricultural productivity and rural development should be further explored.

items.title: AI usage, large language model dependence, and critical thinking among university students: the mediating roles of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED ACOUSTIC ANALYSIS OF LEGAL DISCOURSE PROSODY: OPPORTUNITIES AND LIMITATIONS
items.abstract: The article examines the methodological potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted acoustic analysis for investigating prosody in legal discourse. Prosody is viewed as an essential component of spoken legal communication, shaping the expression of epistemic stance, interpersonal relations, discourse organisation, and persuasive strategies through variations in pitch, intensity, rhythm, pausing, speech rate, and voice quality. The study addresses the limited attention paid to the acoustic dimension of legal discourse and evaluates the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI technologies into prosodic research. The object of the study is the prosodic organisation of spoken legal discourse; the subject is the methodological potential and limitations of AI-assisted acoustic analysis of legal speech. The aim of the study is to provide a criteria-based evaluation of AI-assisted acoustic analysis as a methodological framework for research on legal prosody. The research is theoretical and methodological, drawing on studies in acoustic phonetics, computational paralinguistics, forensic phonetics, legal linguistics, and speech processing. Descriptive, comparative, and criticalevaluative methods are applied to assess AI-assisted acoustic analysis according to six methodological criteria: validity, reliability, scalability, interpretability, ecological validity, and legal and ethical admissibility. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly improves the efficiency, reproducibility, and scalability of acoustic analysis by automating speech preprocessing, feature extraction, and computational modelling, enabling large-scale investigation of authentic legal speech. At the same time, important limitations remain, including reduced ecological validity, limited model transparency, algorithmic bias, risks of overinterpreting acoustic evidence, and legal and ethical concerns. The study argues that AI should complement rather than replace expert phonetic interpretation. It concludes that a human-in-the-loop approach integrating computational technologies with linguistic expertise provides the most reliable framework for future research on legal prosody while ensuring methodological transparency, scientific validity, and legal accountability.

items.title: AI-Assisted ELISA Biomarker Profiling In MASLD: Integrating Early Detection, Risk Stratification, And Treatment Monitoring
items.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most common chronic liver disease worldwide, and its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), now has approved drug treatments. Several circulating biomarkers are measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), including the N-terminal pro-peptide of type III collagen (PRO-C3) and cytokeratin-18 (CK-18) fragments. In this narrative review we ask whether artificial intelligence (AI) can help interpret these ELISA-derived profiles well enough to improve detection of MASLD, fibrosis risk stratification and treatment monitoring beyond what is possible today. We keep the established and the speculative apart. On the established side are the fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index and the ADAPT score, which combines ELISA-measured PRO-C3 with age, diabetes status and platelet count. On the speculative side are machine learning (ML) models for multi-biomarker panels, ML correction of assay artefacts and biomarker-guided choice of drug. CK-18, Fetuin-A and fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) track with disease activity, but none is a validated stand-alone test for MASH. The resmetirom, semaglutide and emricasan trials also remind us that a biomarker moving in the right direction does not prove a patient is better off. We conclude that combining ELISA, AI and precision pharmacotherapy is a reasonable research agenda but not yet a clinical standard, and we set out the validation it still needs.

items.title: AI-Assisted Follow-Up MRI Interpretation in Multiple Sclerosis: Radiology Residents’ Diagnostic Confidence and Performance
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming increasingly utilised in everyday radiological practice. Evaluating follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) is challenging. The aim of this study was to assess changes in confidence among four participating radiology residents when evaluating follow-up MRIs of MS patients using Pixyl.Neuro.MS® software. Methods: This retrospective study included 78 MS patients. Previous and new FLAIR images were independently analysed by four residents, first without AI and then in an immediate AI-assisted second reading using Pixyl.Neuro.MS®, a deep-learning lesion-segmentation software. Readers recorded their findings and confidence after each reading and rated the impact and usefulness of AI. The reference standard was defined by a consensus reading of a neuroradiologist and a radiology resident (15 and 4 years of experience). Paired analyses and patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals were used; bootstrap inference was conditional on the four readers. Results: The reference standard identified 24 patients with new lesions. Mean accuracy across readers increased from 84.62% to 90.71% (difference, 6.09 percentage points; 95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 2.24–10.26). Only Reader 3 showed a significant accuracy increase after Holm adjustment (p = 0.025). No accuracy comparison with routine reports was significant after adjustment. Confidence increased for all readers (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Perceived usefulness did not differ significantly between lesion-burden groups. All readers predominantly rated the impact of AI as positive. The second-reading phase was shorter by a mean of 59.35 s (95% bootstrap CI, 51.39–67.07). Conclusions: In these four residents, the AI-assisted second reading was associated with higher confidence and average accuracy. The immediate sequential design prevents separation of AI contributions from familiarity and order effects, and the shorter second-reading phase does not establish an overall workflow time saving.

items.title: AI-Based Representation of Standardized Chinese Character Copying Deviations for Participant-Level Prediction of Questionnaire-Derived Grit Scores
items.abstract: Repeated template–copy images create a methodological challenge for participant-level prediction because each participant contributes many observations but only one outcome; image-level evaluation can misalign analytical units and permit participant leakage. This study developed a single artificial intelligence (AI) framework with two separately evaluated representation pathways to quantify Chinese character copying deviations and predict questionnaire-derived grit scores. The main cohort included 191 undergraduates (48,826 images), and a non-overlapping same-university validation cohort included 62 participants (13,803 images). The pathways comprised 48-dimensional handcrafted morphological descriptors and shared-weight Siamese deep visual representations. Participant-identity-based partitioning and within-participant aggregation aligned repeated observations with participant-level evaluation. After a held-out comparison of seven backbones, DenseNet121 was selected; subsequent cross-validation estimates were treated as post-selection estimates. In participant-grouped five-fold cross-validation, DenseNet121 achieved mean absolute error (MAE) = 0.233, Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.579, and coefficient of determination (R2) = 0.284, versus 0.279, 0.451, and 0.176 for the handcrafted pathway. In validation, DenseNet121 achieved 0.249, 0.507, and 0.205. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified model-relevant handcrafted features related to spatial ink distribution, character proportion, and texture. The findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for participant-aligned behavioral-image modeling, but prediction remained moderate and incomplete; they do not establish construct-specific measurement, causality, or cross-institutional generalizability.

items.title: AI-Driven CT Analysis for Aortic Disease: A Task-Based Systematic Review of Segmentation, Measurement, and Detection Applications
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography (CTA) are central to assessing aortic aneurysm and dissection, but manual segmentation and geometric analysis remain time-consuming and operator-dependent, while evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) is fragmented. This task-based systematic review synthesised AI applications to CT/CTA of the thoracic and abdominal aorta by primary task: segmentation, measurement, or detection and classification. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC were searched from 2015 to September 2026 following PRISMA 2020; the protocol was registered retrospectively (INPLASY2026110004). Segmentation and measurement studies were appraised with CLAIM and detection studies with QUADAS-2/QUADAS-AI, and results were synthesised without meta-analysis. Results: Of 118 included studies (42 segmentation, 38 measurement, 38 detection), half were published since 2024. Median Dice similarity coefficient was 0.90 or higher for the outer wall, lumen and true and false lumina, but 0.86 for intraluminal thrombus and 0.63 for false lumen thrombus. Automated maximum diameter showed a median absolute bias of 0.26 mm (95% limits of agreement about ±5 mm). Detection of aortic dissection reached a median AUC of 0.96–0.97, mostly in enriched samples. External validation was reported in 14%, 34% and 55% of segmentation, measurement and detection studies, 33 of 38 detection studies were at high risk of bias, and only two systems were evaluated prospectively. Conclusions: AI supports technical automation of aortic CT/CTA segmentation and measurement and is progressing toward multistructure geometric phenotyping and clinical decision support, but independent multicentre validation, consecutive cohorts and prospective reader-in-the-loop studies are required before clinical integration. Detection/classification tools require independent diagnostic and workflow validation.

items.title: AI-Driven EHR and Clinical Decision Support Integration for Reliable, Efficient, and Patient-Centered Care: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are increasingly working together to enhance predictive ability, decision-making, workflow efficiency, and deliver care. But good algorithmic performance is no guarantee of successful clinical integration or patient benefit. Objective The objective of the scoping review was to identify the current evidence regarding the use of AI to enhance EHRs and clinical decision support, exploring clinical applications, EHR integration, reliability and safety, workflow efficiency, patient-centered care and implementation maturity. Methods English language peer-reviewed articles between 2015 and 2026 were searched in 8 multidisciplinary information sources. The search was a combination of concepts involving AI, EHRs/EMRs and clinical decision support/workflow integration. There were 2,028 records identified with 184 being duplicates and 1,844 being screened. Sixty-two full-text reports were assessed for eligibility, of which 16 publications met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Evidence was compiled descriptively and thematically by care delivery domains and a continuum of evidence maturities. Results The types of AI-powered EHR/CDSS applications included risk prediction, early warning, diagnosis and prognosis, triage, treatment and medication support, documentation, and workflow optimization. Technical performance and selected reliability outcomes were best supported by evidence, while prospective evaluation, external validation, sustained deployment in the real-world, and directly measured outcomes from a patient perspective were less well developed. Reported benefits of workflow were noted, but interoperability concerns, alert and cognitive burden, usability, clinician trust, explainability and governance were still key implementation concerns. Conclusion AI has developed from prediction to clinically integrated decision support, but has not reached a level of translational maturity. Systems that are interoperable and prospectively evaluated and systemically human-supervised should be emphasized in future progress, and should be shown to have measurable advantages in safety, efficiency, clinician workflow, patient-centered outcomes, and real-world systems of care delivery.

items.title: AI-Driven Instructional Task Differentiation and Support for Sustainable Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to individualise instruction in secondary technology-enhanced learning environments, yet evidence remains fragmented across modelling approaches and learner outcomes. This systematic review synthesises empirical studies of learner-facing AI-enabled or data-driven technologies that diagnose learner needs and translate them into differentiated feedback, scaffolding, task sequencing, recommendation, assessment, or personalised learning pathways. Searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC identified 3709 records; after filtering and deduplication, 744 records were screened, 84 full texts were assessed, and 46 studies met the eligibility criteria. Evidence was grouped by AI modelling family, differentiated instructional function, learner outcome, and design-based strength. The studies covered six AI modelling families: generative AI and large language models; intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems; recommender systems and learning analytics; automated assessment and diagnostic modelling; agent-based and companion systems; and multimodal, game-based, or AI-XR environments. Twelve studies provided higher-strength comparative or experimental evidence, 17 moderate-strength evidence, and 17 contextual or exploratory evidence. Reported outcomes covered achievement, computational thinking, motivation, engagement, self-regulated learning, cognitive-load management, retention, and system use, with favourable findings alongside mixed or limited evidence. However, unconstrained generative support could reduce productive effort and later learning. The reviewed evidence suggests that timely, interpretable, and pedagogically constrained AI support may contribute to responsive instruction while preserving learner agency. Its long-term sustainability and equity implications remain insufficiently established.

items.title: AI-Driven Malware Detection Using Hybrid CNN-LSTM with Explainable Deep Learning Techniques
items.abstract: Malware detection has become increasingly challenging due to the rapid evolution of sophisticated cyber threats and the limitations of traditional detection techniques. Conventional approaches such as signature-based and heuristic methods are ineffective against zero-day and polymorphic malware, while machine learning models rely heavily on manual feature engineering. Deep learning techniques have improved detection accuracy; however, they often lack interpretability, which is critical for cybersecurity applications. This paper proposes an AI-driven malware detection framework based on a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model integrated with explainable artificial intelligence techniques. The proposed model leverages CNN for spatial feature extraction and LSTM for capturing temporal dependencies in malware behavior, enabling comprehensive analysis of both static and dynamic characteristics. To enhance model transparency, SHAP and LIME are incorporated to provide global and local explanations of predictions. The model is evaluated using benchmark datasets and standard performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed CNN–LSTM model achieves an accuracy of 96.8%, outperforming traditional machine learning models and standalone deep learning approaches. The explainability analysis further confirms that the model relies on meaningful features such as entropy and API call patterns, improving trust and interpretability. The proposed framework provides a robust, accurate, and interpretable solution for malware detection, contributing to the development of trustworthy AI-based cybersecurity systems.

items.title: AI-enabled moxibustion safety: intelligent monitoring and risk prediction
items.abstract: Moxibustion has a broad clinical application base, but its safety is influenced by local temperature, treatment distance, treatment duration, combustion status, and individual thermal tolerance. Conventional safety management mainly relies on practitioner experience and patients’ subjective heat perception, making continuous quantification and dynamic adjustment during treatment difficult. In recent years, artificial intelligence, computer vision, infrared thermography, intelligent sensing, and robotic technologies have increasingly been applied to moxibustion, enabling acupoint recognition, temperature monitoring, spatial localization, trajectory planning, and feedback control to improve treatment visualization and controllability and to promote a transition from fixed-parameter operation toward dynamic closed-loop regulation. Current evidence mainly supports functions related to acupoint localization, real-time monitoring, and automated control, while some robotic systems have also demonstrated standardized operation and temperature-regulation capabilities. However, models that directly predict clinical adverse events such as burns and blisters remain insufficiently validated, and individualized parameter optimization and home-based remote management are still largely exploratory, with their actual clinical safety benefits not yet established. Future studies should further standardize safety outcomes and monitoring parameters, establish multicenter large-sample adverse-event databases, and strengthen external model validation, risk calibration, and evaluation of device fail-safe protection. This review summarizes advances in AI-enabled intelligent monitoring and risk prediction for moxibustion and examines the evidence base, application boundaries, and future directions of intelligent safety management, with the aim of informing more intelligent and precise moxibustion safety management.

items.title: AI-to-AI Communication: Toward a New Paradigm of Intelligence Search
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has transformed the way people search for and interact with information. Traditional search engines primarily retrieve documents, web pages, and other information sources, while modern large language models can interpret questions, reason over information, and generate answers. This paper explores a possible next step: a search paradigm in which AI agents communicate with one another to search for, compare, evaluate, and synthesize answers. This paper proposes an AI-to-AI communication paradigm for intelligence search, extending information retrieval beyond the conventional interaction between a user and a single AI model to a collaborative process involving multiple specialized AI systems. Rather than merely collecting or aggregating their responses, the framework enables participating systems to independently investigate a query, retrieve relevant evidence, exchange findings, and critically assess one another's contributions. The resulting intelligence is evaluated and integrated to construct a well-supported response. A key distinction of the proposed architecture is its shift from answer-level agreement to claim-level verification. Instead of treating each AI-generated response as a single unit, the architecture decomposes responses into individual claims, independently retrieves supporting evidence, evaluates source independence, and accounts for dependencies among potential errors. This process enables the final synthesis to consider not only the agreement among AI systems but also the evidential support, credibility, and potential dependence underlying their claims. The numerical results provide initial evidence that the proposed framework can support a new architectural layer between AI systems, dedicated to discovering, coordinating, evaluating, and verifying distributed machine intelligence. By enabling structured interaction and evidence-based assessment across multiple AI systems, this layer offers a foundation for moving beyond isolated AI capabilities toward more coordinated and reliable forms of machine intelligence.
